newsitem.title: UK: Mark off high but firm as Tietmeyer gives boost.
newsitem.headline: Mark off high but firm as Tietmeyer gives boost.

text.p: The mark was on a firm footing against other European currencies in late trade, after getting a boost all around from mark-supportive comments made by Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer.

His comment that the dollar's correction phase against the mark was over shored the mark up against major currencies after it hit a 41-month low against the dollar and 23-month low on the yen earlier in the day.
The central bank chief also said it was important for the mark to stay strong and enter European monetary union as a strong currency.

"When he (Tietmeyer) said the dollar's correction against the mark was more or less finished, he caught the market on the hop because people were quite short on the mark. So there was a lot of buying across the board," said one trader at a U.S. bank.
The mark was at 3.3798/00 French francs at 1430 GMT, off its session highs of 3.3821 but well above its late Wednesday European level of 3.3741/46.
It was also firm on the lira at 976.40/70 against 974.10/60.
"The tone he used was a bit sharp, a slight stepping up of the rhetoric," said Klaus Baader, currency economist at Lehman Brothers here.
"It seems the Bundesbank's benign neglect towards the weakness of the mark that has been predominating up to now is abating a bit," he said.
The mark had already been gaining on the crosses before Tietmeyer's comments, made after the Bundesbank's annual out-of-town council meeting, due to renewed fears over EMU.
Nervousness about Germany's and France's ability to meet EMU budget-deficit criteria had surfaced ahead of the presentation on Friday of Bonn's 1997 supplementary budget and 1998 budget proposals.

Matters had not been helped by a report in the French daily La Tribune that the audit of France's public finances, due on July 21, would show a budget deficit-to-GDP ratio of 3.6-3.7 percent in 1997. The French finance ministry declined comment.
Meanwhile, German government sources said the budget deficit would total 110 billion marks, hitting the EMU criteria target spot-on at 3.0 percent of GDP.
However, the mark crosses showed little reaction to this.
"Concerning the budget numbers, we'll just have to wait and see what comes out. Tietmeyer's really taken the limelight for the moment," the U.S. bank trader said.

The mark had also been bolstered on the crosses earlier by vague speculation that the Bundesbank might decide to switch to a variable repo rate. Traders and analysts had said such a change in policy would herald higher German interest rates, although they added that the idea was a bit far-fetched.
But the Bundesbank kept its repo tenders at a fixed rate and its key interest rates steady, and the mark edged lower.
"People have been very short in the mark on the crosses for quite some time, and such rumours would make a good excuse (to buy marks)," said Ernesto Ramirez, European economist at Bankers Trust here.

Elsewhere, sterling slipped from near its six-year high against the mark after the Bank of England raised its key base rate to 6.75 percent from 6.50. The rate hike had been well anticipated, but sterling slipped as the market was disappointed at the small size of the rate hike.
The Netherlands also raised rates today, pushing its special advances rate up by 10 basis points to 2.90 percent.

The guilder stayed steady at 1.125850/925 to the mark against 1.1259/60 late on Wednesday. It was dollar/mark which took the brunt of the impact from the Dutch rate hike, dropping briefly to its session low.
-- Chizu Nomiyama, London Forex Desk, +44-171-542-6721
